I reviewed the uploaded advisor handout and checked additional NBV / active reconstruction / value-learning sources. Overall: the proposal is now much stronger. It has a coherent thesis spine, a leakage-safe formal model, explicit evidence gates, and a clearer distinction between thesis-core finite-candidate Q_H and later online/continuous-control work. The main remaining issue is that the technical design section is now almost too rich: it risks turning a focused advisor-facing contract into a long architecture wishlist. I would sharpen the proposal by separating core thesis commitments from ablation / bridge ideas more aggressively. High-level verdict The scientific core is good: Target-specific point-mesh RRI + actor-visible target descriptor + finite valid candidate table + oracle lookahead headroom + masked finite-horizon Q_{H,\theta} evaluated by oracle re-scoring. That is a defensible thesis. The handout explicitly says the current implemented substrate has scene-level oracle RRI, finite candidate tables, EVL/EFM context, and a VIN-style scorer, but not yet target-specific supervision, actor-visible target selection, trusted rollouts, or a learned finite-horizon value model. That is exactly the right “known vs. unknown” boundary for advisor discussion. ￼ The strongest improvement is the dependency-chain framing: RQ1 objective, RQ2 target/matching, RQ3 candidate/rollout support, RQ4 headroom and Q_H, RQ5 scaling, RQ6 online/continuous escalation. The line “later questions should not be used to rescue failed earlier contracts” is excellent because it prevents scope drift. ￼ The biggest remaining risk is that the proposal simultaneously says “first implementation” and then includes residual dueling Q_H, ROIAlign3D target tokens, R6D+LFF pose features, QCNet-style relative positional encoding, S^2 directional memory, spherical-harmonic ablations, Set Transformer candidate encoding, distributional heads, GNNs, privileged-teacher distillation, and online/continuous bridges. That is scientifically interesting, but too many of those sound like deliverables. The text should make the minimal Q_H baseline unmistakable and move the rest into a staged ablation ladder. ￼ ⸻ 1. Thesis claim: strong, but make the success criterion more explicit Your current claim says ARIA-NBV should measure target-specific point-mesh improvement, test oracle lookahead headroom over myopic selection, and train actor-visible Q_H to recover that headroom under oracle re-evaluation. That is very strong. ￼ I would add one sentence immediately after the claim: The thesis succeeds quantitatively only if the learned actor-visible policy \(\pi_Q\) improves over the learned myopic target scorer when oracle lookahead shows positive headroom; if no headroom exists, the thesis reports a negative planning result for the evaluated candidate distribution, horizon, branch factor, target set, and split. Why: the current text already says something similar in the risk section, but placing it near the thesis claim prevents a reader from asking, “What exactly counts as success?” Your risk section correctly says that if \Delta_{\text{look}} is near zero, you report no measurable non-myopic headroom for the evaluated split, target set, horizon, branch factor, and candidate distribution. ￼ ⸻ 2. Formal model: good leakage separation; clarify whether this is an MDP, POMDP, or controlled replay process The state separation is one of the proposal’s best scientific decisions. You define logged historic state s_t^{hist}, counterfactual actor state s_t^{cf0}, and privileged oracle state s_t^{oracle}, and explicitly state that the real egocentric trajectory modalities differ from the geometry-only state available after synthetic view choices. ￼ However, I would soften “finite-horizon MDP” slightly. The candidate table is regenerated after each selected action, target selection is stochastic/top-K/temperature-softmax, and the EVL field is frozen at the root while only the geometry proxy updates. This is a masked finite-horizon candidate replay process and can be treated as an MDP after fixing the candidate generator, RNG seed, root snippet, target, and transition rule, but the raw formulation is not a standard fully observable MDP. Suggested replacement: The first non-myopic experiment is a finite-horizon masked candidate-decision process. After fixing the root snippet, target, candidate generator, and RNG seed, it can be treated as an MDP over valid candidate indices; without those fixtures, it is better viewed as a controlled replay process with stochastic candidate regeneration. This is more scientifically careful and avoids a reviewer objecting that s_t^{cf0} is not a full Markov state. ⸻ 3. Target matching: very good, but add thresholds and failure categories The target protocol is now crisp: V0 uses GT OBB input only for sanity/upper-bound, while V1 uses OBS-SEL / PRED-Q / GT-EVAL so that target selection and Q_H conditioning are actor-visible and GT OBBs/crops are labels/evaluation only. ￼ The match score \mu(\hat e,e) is useful, especially the top-1/top-2 gap g_\mu. The current text says unmatched, unsupported, or ambiguous targets are target-invalid protocol cases rather than low target-RRI examples. That is exactly right. ￼ I would sharpen it with explicit decision thresholds, even if placeholders: Accept a match only if \[ \kappa(\hat y_{\hat e}, y_e)=1,\quad \mu_1 \ge \tau_{\mu},\quad g_\mu = \mu_1-\mu_2 \ge \tau_{gap},\quad n^{semi}_{\hat e}+n^{EVL}_{\hat e} \ge \tau_{support}. \] The advisor decision is not whether to threshold, but which thresholds define the validated target subset. This turns the matching protocol from a scoring idea into a reproducible filter. ⸻ 4. RRI and endpoint metrics: strong; add a mesh-sampling caveat The target error model is now coherent. You define C_e(\mathcal P_t), target error \Delta_t^e, immediate target RRI r_t^e, cumulative return G_t^{(H)}, endpoint gain J_e^{(H)}, and log gain J_{e,\log}^{(H)}. You also explicitly state that cumulative RRI is not algebraically identical to endpoint gain because each immediate RRI is normalized by the current target error. This resolves a major ambiguity from earlier drafts. ￼ One scientific caveat is missing: mesh-to-point completeness averaged over triangles can be biased by mesh tessellation unless it is area-weighted or evaluated over uniformly sampled surface points. Your previous seminar paper describes point-to-triangle and triangle-to-point distances, but the proposal should state how tessellation bias is controlled. ￼ Suggested sentence: For completeness, triangle-to-point terms should be area-weighted or evaluated on uniformly sampled target-surface points so that target-RRI is not biased by mesh tessellation density. ⸻ 5. CORAL interface: fix a likely mathematical error This is the most important concrete correction. The advisor handout currently says: \mathbf c^{CORAL}_{t,i}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf o^{CORAL}_{t,i}), \qquad \hat r^e_\psi=\operatorname{calib}(\mathbf c^{CORAL}_{t,i}) But CORAL logits are threshold logits, not class logits. Your own previous paper text correctly states that CORAL produces K-1 cumulative probabilities p_k=P(y>k), and these are not class marginals; to recover a scalar RRI estimate, you convert cumulative probabilities into class marginals \pi_k=p_{k-1}-p_k, with p_{-1}=1 and p_{K-1}=0, then compute \hat r=\sum_k \pi_k u_k. ￼ Replace Eq. 20 with: \[ p_{t,i,k}=\sigma(o^{CORAL}_{t,i,k}),\qquad \pi_{t,i,k}=p_{t,i,k-1}-p_{t,i,k},\quad p_{t,i,-1}=1,\;p_{t,i,K-1}=0, \] \[ \hat r^e_\psi(s_t^{cf0},z_e,q_{t,i}) = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\pi_{t,i,k}u_k. \] Then say: CORAL threshold probabilities may be passed as candidate features, but they are not softmax class probabilities. This is a small edit with high scientific payoff. ⸻ 6. Planned value model: good idea, but reduce architecture overcommitment The residual idea is strong: Q_{H,\theta} = \hat r^e_\psi + A^H_\theta It gives a clean interpretation: Q_H starts near the myopic scorer and only learns non-myopic corrections when rollouts justify them. ￼ The dueling extension is also well motivated because dueling networks explicitly separate a state-value estimator from action advantages, which is useful when many actions have similar values; that fits finite candidate sets with many near-duplicate candidate views. ￼ But the handout currently has both a residual equation and a later residual-dueling equation. Keep the dueling version as the single canonical definition: \[ Q_{H,\theta}(s_t^{cf0},z_e,q_{t,i}) = \hat r^e_\psi(s_t^{cf0},z_e,q_{t,i}) + V_\theta(s_t^{cf0},z_e,H_t) + A^H_{\theta,i} - \frac{1}{|\mathcal A_t|} \sum_{j\in\mathcal A_t} A^H_{\theta,j}. \] Then make the training order explicit: Stage 1: train/calibrate the myopic scorer \(\hat r^e_\psi\). Stage 2: freeze or slowly fine-tune \(\hat r^e_\psi\) while training the residual \(Q_H\). Stage 3: ablate whether end-to-end fine-tuning improves oracle-evaluated policy performance. This prevents a failure mode where \hat r_\psi and A_\theta both move and the residual interpretation disappears. ⸻ 7. Candidate-set encoder: cite Set Transformer, but make it one option The proposal states that candidate reasoning must be permutation-equivariant and plans a Set Transformer candidate encoder. That is well supported: Set Transformer was designed for set-structured inputs and uses attention to model interactions among set elements while preserving permutation structure. ￼ However, for advisor-facing scope, I would say: The first implementation uses a permutation-equivariant candidate-set encoder (Set Transformer or masked self-attention over candidate tokens). A no-interaction candidate MLP and a pooled DeepSets baseline are required ablations. Why: if N_q is small and candidate rows are already highly informative, a Set Transformer might not beat a simpler masked candidate MLP. A reviewer will trust the result more if the architecture is justified by an ablation. ⸻ 8. QCNet-style relative encoding: good inspiration, but frame it as ablation, not core QCNet’s query-centric idea is useful because it encodes relations in the query’s local coordinate frame and aims to reuse invariant scene features rather than re-normalizing everything globally. ￼ For ARIA-NBV, this should be an ablation, not the default thesis risk. Keep the idea, but narrow it: The default candidate token uses relative pose to the target and selected-history summaries. QCNet-style candidate-local pairwise RPE is the first candidate-set interaction ablation. This keeps the proposal sharp and avoids sounding like you are porting a trajectory prediction architecture wholesale. ⸻ 9. Directional memory: excellent, but separate “visibility novelty” from “pose relation” Your directional S^2 memory is one of the strongest novel design elements. The text correctly says QCNet-style RPE is a pairwise pose-relation signal, while S^2 memory summarizes accumulated viewing directions for target-local cells. ￼ The second-moment memory is a good first implementation. The spherical-harmonic version should remain an ablation, as your text already suggests. I would add one evaluation metric: Directional-memory ablations should report not only endpoint \(J_e^{(H)}\), but also whether selected views increase angular diversity around the matched target crop. This makes the directional memory empirically testable, not just architecturally plausible. ⸻ 10. Learning objective and evaluation: strong; add all-valid-candidate vs selected-transition distinction The masked Double-Q backup is a good first value-learning method. Double Q-learning is directly relevant because it addresses overestimation from max-based value targets, which is exactly the risk when bootstrapping over a finite candidate table. ￼ Your evaluation contract is also strong: Q_H is not interpreted as planning until the one-step scorer passes ranking, oracle-evaluated selected rollouts, calibration/stage-shift diagnostics, and Rerun examples; selected actions are re-evaluated under identical roots, candidate budgets, and acquisition budgets. ￼ One ambiguity remains: do you train Q_H on only selected-action rows, or on all valid candidate rows? Immediate target RRI may be available for all candidates at a node, but successor states are only materialized for selected/expanded candidates. Clarify: The one-step scorer is trained on all valid candidate rows with oracle immediate target-RRI labels. The finite-horizon \(Q_H\) backup is trained on expanded transition rows for which the successor candidate table and terminal flag are materialized. If all-candidate successor expansion is unavailable, non-expanded candidates contribute only immediate/myopic supervision, not bootstrapped \(Q_H\) targets. This prevents a common offline-RL ambiguity. ⸻ 11. Evidence table: excellent; add confidence intervals / paired tests The compact evidence contract and leakage-aware policy table are very strong. They require scorer ranking evidence, candidate/replay provenance, with/without-mask metrics, seed metadata, shuffled-candidate evaluation, scene-level splits, no silent coverage changes, and Zarr/LRZ gates. ￼ Add one statistical reporting rule: All policy comparisons should be paired by root snippet, target, candidate seed, and horizon; report mean, median, bootstrap confidence intervals, and per-scene win rates for \(J_e^{(H)}\), \(G_t^{(H)}\), and invalidity. This is especially important because the thesis may operate on a subset if full 100-scene scale is blocked. ⸻ 12. Roadmap and risks: strong; add an advisor decision box near the front The risk section is well written: if M1 geometry/oracle labels fail, the thesis becomes validation + one-step scoring; if target matching is sparse/ambiguous, report target RRI only on validated subsets; if \Delta_{\text{look}} is near zero, report no measurable non-myopic headroom for the evaluated setup. The open advisor decisions are also narrow and appropriate. ￼ Move the “open advisor decisions” near the front, ideally as a boxed list after the thesis claim: Advisor decisions requested: 1. target-match acceptance protocol, 2. final scene-level split, 3. first actor-visible crop descriptor, 4. CORAL-to-\(Q_H\) interface, 5. final evidence scale / subset rule, 6. escalation rule for online-discrete or continuous control. This will make the handout more useful in the actual meeting. ⸻ Research sources to add or reposition A. Add SCONE for surface-coverage lookahead, but keep it as contrast SCONE is a useful source to add because it tries to maximize surface metrics by Monte Carlo integration over a volumetric representation and uses attention to predict visibility/gain for candidate poses in large scenes. It supports your argument that candidate utility can be learned over volumetric/point evidence, but it is coverage/surface-gain oriented, not target point-mesh RRI. ￼ Use it for: SCONE motivates candidate visibility/gain prediction over volumetric evidence, but ARIA-NBV keeps point-mesh target-RRI as the supervised utility. Suggested BibTeX key: SCONE-guedon2022. B. Add MACARONS for online RGB-only mapping as boundary, not core MACARONS learns mapping and coverage anticipation from RGB online self-supervision and is relevant to “what if we want online/RGB-only exploration later.” It is useful as a bridge source, not as thesis-core evidence, because your thesis relies on ASE mesh-supervised oracle target-RRI. ￼ Use it for: MACARONS is a bridge reference for online/RGB-only coverage anticipation; it does not replace mesh-supervised target-RRI labels. Suggested BibTeX key: MACARONS-guedon2023. C. Update Hestia citation to WACV 2026 accepted paper Your handout already cites Hestia, but the accepted WACV 2026 open-access entry is stronger than just a project page. The WACV page says Hestia improves RL-based five-degree-of-freedom viewpoint prediction using a hierarchical structure, close-greedy strategy, face-aware design, and reports real-time inference plus robustness to object placement. ￼ Use it to justify only the post-Q_H bridge: Hestia motivates target/look-at then feasible-pose factorization and directional face/visibility memory, but ARIA-NBV does not adopt its coverage reward as the thesis objective. D. Keep Set Transformer, but add a simpler baseline Set Transformer is appropriate because candidate tables are unordered sets and interactions among candidate rows matter. But to avoid overclaiming, add DeepSets or a masked candidate MLP baseline. Your references.bib already appears to include DeepSets and Set Transformer, so this is mostly a writing change. Set Transformer’s own motivation is permutation-invariant set processing with attention-based interactions. ￼ Use it for: Permutation-equivariant candidate reasoning is justified, but the required ablation is no-interaction candidate scoring vs pooled-set interaction. E. Keep Dueling DQN, but say why it fits finite candidates Dueling DQN is well aligned because it decomposes value and advantage and is especially useful when many actions have similar values. Your proposal’s finite candidate table will often contain many plausible near-duplicates, so this is a very good source. ￼ Suggested proposal sentence: The dueling head is justified because finite candidate tables often contain many similar-valued actions; the value stream captures scene-target-history context while the advantage stream captures candidate-specific corrections. F. Add prioritized replay only if rare high-RRI transitions are a real issue I would not add prioritized replay as core. But if rollout traces are extremely imbalanced, you can cite it as an ablation for rare high-return transitions. Keep it optional. Suggested language: If high-RRI or high-headroom transitions are rare, prioritized sampling of replay rows is an ablation, not a default training assumption. G. Use object-centric 3DGS NBV as motivation, not methodology The object-centric 3DGS NBV preprint is useful because it independently supports target/object-specific view selection in cluttered scenes, but it should not reshape the thesis toward 3DGS. The paper is recent and target-relevant, but its representation and task setup differ from your ASE/EVL point-mesh RRI setting. The search result describes object-centric NBV for object-aware 3DGS in cluttered scenes, focusing views on target objects and reporting depth-error reductions. ￼ Use it for: Recent object-centric 3DGS NBV supports the importance of target-conditioned view utility, but ARIA-NBV uses EVL/ASE point-mesh target-RRI rather than 3DGS uncertainty as supervision. ⸻ Proposed RQ sharpening I would keep six RQs, but make them maximally crisp: RQ1 Objective and metrics: Can target-conditioned finite-candidate NBV improve endpoint target quality under equal budget while training on additive target-RRI returns? RQ2 Target and matching: Can actor-visible target descriptors and deterministic GT matching produce leakage-safe target-RRI labels at sufficient coverage? RQ3 Candidate and rollout support: Do mixed target-centric/exploration candidates and stochastic rollout support produce enough valid, diverse, non-myopic training data? RQ4 Oracle headroom and \(Q_H\): Does bounded oracle lookahead expose non-myopic headroom, and can masked residual dueling \(Q_H\) recover it over the learned myopic scorer? RQ5 Scaling: Which scale path preserves the same mesh/oracle target-RRI contract beyond small trusted subsets? RQ6 Escalation: Only after RQ1-RQ5 pass, is online discrete interaction or continuous target-then-pose control scientifically justified? This is very close to what you have, but it emphasizes “sufficient coverage” and “non-myopic training data” in RQ2/RQ3, which are likely the real thesis risks. ⸻ Suggested objective rewrite Current objective is implied across the handout. I would make it explicit as: The objective is not to build a general continuous-control NBV agent. The objective is to test whether the existing ASE/EVL/VIN substrate can support a leakage-safe target-conditioned finite-candidate planning result. The required evidence is: validated target-RRI labels, actor-visible target matching, a calibrated myopic target scorer, measured oracle-lookahead headroom, and an oracle-evaluated actor-visible \(Q_{H,\theta}\) policy that recovers measurable headroom when such headroom exists. This removes ambiguity and makes your advisor-facing claim very hard to misread. ⸻ Concrete edits I would make now 1. Fix CORAL Eq. 20: replace softmax with sigmoid threshold probabilities and cumulative-to-marginal conversion. This is the only clear mathematical bug I see. ￼ 2. Move advisor decisions to page 1: final split, target-match thresholds, CORAL-to-Q_H, crop descriptor, evidence scale, escalation substrate. ￼ 3. Rename “MDP” to “masked finite-horizon candidate-decision process,” then say it becomes an MDP under fixed generator/RNG/root assumptions. 4. Collapse the value-model section into Core / Ablations / Bridges: * Core: target scorer, residual dueling Q_H, masked Double-Q, Set Transformer or candidate-set attention. * Ablations: QCNet RPE, S^2 memory, spherical harmonics, distributional heads, GNNs. * Bridges: online discrete, continuous target-then-pose, simulator-backed actor-critic. 5. Add SCONE and MACARONS as “coverage/online contrast” sources, not thesis-core methods. ￼ 6. Update Hestia citation to the WACV 2026 open-access paper. ￼ 7. Add area-weighting / surface-sampling caveat for target-mesh completeness. 8. Define all target-match thresholds as advisor decisions rather than leaving matching purely descriptive. 9. Add paired statistical reporting: paired by root snippet, target, seed, candidate budget, horizon; report confidence intervals and scene-level win rates. 10. Clarify training data for Q_H: all valid candidates for one-step labels; only expanded/materialized successor rows for bootstrapped finite-horizon targets. ⸻ Bottom line The proposal is scientifically coherent and much more mature than the earlier question drafts. The thesis spine is now defensible: quality-driven, target-conditioned, finite-candidate planning under strict leakage controls. The main next step is not to add more architecture. It is to make the proposal sharper by marking the minimal success path: \text{target-RRI} \rightarrow \text{actor-visible target descriptor} \rightarrow \text{myopic scorer} \rightarrow \Delta_{\text{look}} \rightarrow Q_{H,\theta}\text{ recovery} Everything else—QCNet-style RPE, S^2 memory, spherical harmonics, GNNs, distributional heads, IQL, continuous target-then-pose, 3DGS, SceneScript—should be clearly labeled as ablation or bridge, not the thesis success criterion.

Target-specific point-mesh RRI + actor-visible target descriptor + finite valid candidate table + oracle lookahead headroom + masked finite-horizon Q_{H,\theta} evaluated by oracle re-scoring.

That is a defensible thesis. The handout explicitly says the current implemented substrate has scene-level oracle RRI, finite candidate tables, EVL/EFM context, and a VIN-style scorer, but not yet target-specific supervision, actor-visible target selection, trusted rollouts, or a learned finite-horizon value model. That is exactly the right “known vs. unknown” boundary for advisor discussion.  ￼

The strongest improvement is the dependency-chain framing: RQ1 objective, RQ2 target/matching, RQ3 candidate/rollout support, RQ4 headroom and Q_H, RQ5 scaling, RQ6 online/continuous escalation. The line “later questions should not be used to rescue failed earlier contracts” is excellent because it prevents scope drift.  ￼

The biggest remaining risk is that the proposal simultaneously says “first implementation” and then includes residual dueling Q_H, ROIAlign3D target tokens, R6D+LFF pose features, QCNet-style relative positional encoding, S^2 directional memory, spherical-harmonic ablations, Set Transformer candidate encoding, distributional heads, GNNs, privileged-teacher distillation, and online/continuous bridges. That is scientifically interesting, but too many of those sound like deliverables. The text should make the minimal Q_H baseline unmistakable and move the rest into a staged ablation ladder.  ￼

⸻

1. Thesis claim: strong, but make the success criterion more explicit

Your current claim says ARIA-NBV should measure target-specific point-mesh improvement, test oracle lookahead headroom over myopic selection, and train actor-visible Q_H to recover that headroom under oracle re-evaluation. That is very strong.  ￼

I would add one sentence immediately after the claim:

The thesis succeeds quantitatively only if the learned actor-visible policy
\(\pi_Q\) improves over the learned myopic target scorer when oracle lookahead
shows positive headroom; if no headroom exists, the thesis reports a negative
planning result for the evaluated candidate distribution, horizon, branch
factor, target set, and split.

Why: the current text already says something similar in the risk section, but placing it near the thesis claim prevents a reader from asking, “What exactly counts as success?” Your risk section correctly says that if \Delta_{\text{look}} is near zero, you report no measurable non-myopic headroom for the evaluated split, target set, horizon, branch factor, and candidate distribution.  ￼

⸻

2. Formal model: good leakage separation; clarify whether this is an MDP, POMDP, or controlled replay process

The state separation is one of the proposal’s best scientific decisions. You define logged historic state s_t^{hist}, counterfactual actor state s_t^{cf0}, and privileged oracle state s_t^{oracle}, and explicitly state that the real egocentric trajectory modalities differ from the geometry-only state available after synthetic view choices.  ￼

However, I would soften “finite-horizon MDP” slightly. The candidate table is regenerated after each selected action, target selection is stochastic/top-K/temperature-softmax, and the EVL field is frozen at the root while only the geometry proxy updates. This is a masked finite-horizon candidate replay process and can be treated as an MDP after fixing the candidate generator, RNG seed, root snippet, target, and transition rule, but the raw formulation is not a standard fully observable MDP.

Suggested replacement:

The first non-myopic experiment is a finite-horizon masked candidate-decision
process. After fixing the root snippet, target, candidate generator, and RNG
seed, it can be treated as an MDP over valid candidate indices; without those
fixtures, it is better viewed as a controlled replay process with stochastic
candidate regeneration.

This is more scientifically careful and avoids a reviewer objecting that s_t^{cf0} is not a full Markov state.

⸻

3. Target matching: very good, but add thresholds and failure categories

The target protocol is now crisp: V0 uses GT OBB input only for sanity/upper-bound, while V1 uses OBS-SEL / PRED-Q / GT-EVAL so that target selection and Q_H conditioning are actor-visible and GT OBBs/crops are labels/evaluation only.  ￼

The match score \mu(\hat e,e) is useful, especially the top-1/top-2 gap g_\mu. The current text says unmatched, unsupported, or ambiguous targets are target-invalid protocol cases rather than low target-RRI examples. That is exactly right.  ￼

I would sharpen it with explicit decision thresholds, even if placeholders:

Accept a match only if
\[
\kappa(\hat y_{\hat e}, y_e)=1,\quad
\mu_1 \ge \tau_{\mu},\quad
g_\mu = \mu_1-\mu_2 \ge \tau_{gap},\quad
n^{semi}_{\hat e}+n^{EVL}_{\hat e} \ge \tau_{support}.
\]
The advisor decision is not whether to threshold, but which thresholds define
the validated target subset.

This turns the matching protocol from a scoring idea into a reproducible filter.

⸻

4. RRI and endpoint metrics: strong; add a mesh-sampling caveat

The target error model is now coherent. You define C_e(\mathcal P_t), target error \Delta_t^e, immediate target RRI r_t^e, cumulative return G_t^{(H)}, endpoint gain J_e^{(H)}, and log gain J_{e,\log}^{(H)}. You also explicitly state that cumulative RRI is not algebraically identical to endpoint gain because each immediate RRI is normalized by the current target error. This resolves a major ambiguity from earlier drafts.  ￼

One scientific caveat is missing: mesh-to-point completeness averaged over triangles can be biased by mesh tessellation unless it is area-weighted or evaluated over uniformly sampled surface points. Your previous seminar paper describes point-to-triangle and triangle-to-point distances, but the proposal should state how tessellation bias is controlled.  ￼

Suggested sentence:

For completeness, triangle-to-point terms should be area-weighted or evaluated
on uniformly sampled target-surface points so that target-RRI is not biased by
mesh tessellation density.

⸻

5. CORAL interface: fix a likely mathematical error

This is the most important concrete correction.

The advisor handout currently says:

\mathbf c^{CORAL}_{t,i}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf o^{CORAL}_{t,i}),
\qquad
\hat r^e_\psi=\operatorname{calib}(\mathbf c^{CORAL}_{t,i})

But CORAL logits are threshold logits, not class logits. Your own previous paper text correctly states that CORAL produces K-1 cumulative probabilities p_k=P(y>k), and these are not class marginals; to recover a scalar RRI estimate, you convert cumulative probabilities into class marginals \pi_k=p_{k-1}-p_k, with p_{-1}=1 and p_{K-1}=0, then compute \hat r=\sum_k \pi_k u_k.  ￼

Replace Eq. 20 with:

\[
p_{t,i,k}=\sigma(o^{CORAL}_{t,i,k}),\qquad
\pi_{t,i,k}=p_{t,i,k-1}-p_{t,i,k},\quad
p_{t,i,-1}=1,\;p_{t,i,K-1}=0,
\]
\[
\hat r^e_\psi(s_t^{cf0},z_e,q_{t,i})
=
\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\pi_{t,i,k}u_k.
\]

Then say:

CORAL threshold probabilities may be passed as candidate features, but they are
not softmax class probabilities.

This is a small edit with high scientific payoff.

⸻

6. Planned value model: good idea, but reduce architecture overcommitment

The residual idea is strong:

Q_{H,\theta} = \hat r^e_\psi + A^H_\theta

It gives a clean interpretation: Q_H starts near the myopic scorer and only learns non-myopic corrections when rollouts justify them.  ￼

The dueling extension is also well motivated because dueling networks explicitly separate a state-value estimator from action advantages, which is useful when many actions have similar values; that fits finite candidate sets with many near-duplicate candidate views.  ￼

But the handout currently has both a residual equation and a later residual-dueling equation. Keep the dueling version as the single canonical definition:

\[
Q_{H,\theta}(s_t^{cf0},z_e,q_{t,i})
=
\hat r^e_\psi(s_t^{cf0},z_e,q_{t,i})
+
V_\theta(s_t^{cf0},z_e,H_t)
+
A^H_{\theta,i}
-
\frac{1}{|\mathcal A_t|}
\sum_{j\in\mathcal A_t} A^H_{\theta,j}.
\]

Then make the training order explicit:

Stage 1: train/calibrate the myopic scorer \(\hat r^e_\psi\).
Stage 2: freeze or slowly fine-tune \(\hat r^e_\psi\) while training the residual \(Q_H\).
Stage 3: ablate whether end-to-end fine-tuning improves oracle-evaluated policy performance.

This prevents a failure mode where \hat r_\psi and A_\theta both move and the residual interpretation disappears.

⸻

7. Candidate-set encoder: cite Set Transformer, but make it one option

The proposal states that candidate reasoning must be permutation-equivariant and plans a Set Transformer candidate encoder. That is well supported: Set Transformer was designed for set-structured inputs and uses attention to model interactions among set elements while preserving permutation structure.  ￼

However, for advisor-facing scope, I would say:

The first implementation uses a permutation-equivariant candidate-set encoder
(Set Transformer or masked self-attention over candidate tokens). A no-interaction
candidate MLP and a pooled DeepSets baseline are required ablations.

Why: if N_q is small and candidate rows are already highly informative, a Set Transformer might not beat a simpler masked candidate MLP. A reviewer will trust the result more if the architecture is justified by an ablation.

⸻

8. QCNet-style relative encoding: good inspiration, but frame it as ablation, not core

QCNet’s query-centric idea is useful because it encodes relations in the query’s local coordinate frame and aims to reuse invariant scene features rather than re-normalizing everything globally.  ￼

For ARIA-NBV, this should be an ablation, not the default thesis risk. Keep the idea, but narrow it:

The default candidate token uses relative pose to the target and selected-history
summaries. QCNet-style candidate-local pairwise RPE is the first candidate-set
interaction ablation.

This keeps the proposal sharp and avoids sounding like you are porting a trajectory prediction architecture wholesale.

⸻

9. Directional memory: excellent, but separate “visibility novelty” from “pose relation”

Your directional S^2 memory is one of the strongest novel design elements. The text correctly says QCNet-style RPE is a pairwise pose-relation signal, while S^2 memory summarizes accumulated viewing directions for target-local cells.  ￼

The second-moment memory is a good first implementation. The spherical-harmonic version should remain an ablation, as your text already suggests. I would add one evaluation metric:

Directional-memory ablations should report not only endpoint \(J_e^{(H)}\), but
also whether selected views increase angular diversity around the matched target
crop.

This makes the directional memory empirically testable, not just architecturally plausible.

⸻

10. Learning objective and evaluation: strong; add all-valid-candidate vs selected-transition distinction

The masked Double-Q backup is a good first value-learning method. Double Q-learning is directly relevant because it addresses overestimation from max-based value targets, which is exactly the risk when bootstrapping over a finite candidate table.  ￼

Your evaluation contract is also strong: Q_H is not interpreted as planning until the one-step scorer passes ranking, oracle-evaluated selected rollouts, calibration/stage-shift diagnostics, and Rerun examples; selected actions are re-evaluated under identical roots, candidate budgets, and acquisition budgets.  ￼

One ambiguity remains: do you train Q_H on only selected-action rows, or on all valid candidate rows? Immediate target RRI may be available for all candidates at a node, but successor states are only materialized for selected/expanded candidates. Clarify:

The one-step scorer is trained on all valid candidate rows with oracle immediate
target-RRI labels. The finite-horizon \(Q_H\) backup is trained on expanded
transition rows for which the successor candidate table and terminal flag are
materialized. If all-candidate successor expansion is unavailable, non-expanded
candidates contribute only immediate/myopic supervision, not bootstrapped
\(Q_H\) targets.

This prevents a common offline-RL ambiguity.

⸻

11. Evidence table: excellent; add confidence intervals / paired tests

The compact evidence contract and leakage-aware policy table are very strong. They require scorer ranking evidence, candidate/replay provenance, with/without-mask metrics, seed metadata, shuffled-candidate evaluation, scene-level splits, no silent coverage changes, and Zarr/LRZ gates.  ￼

Add one statistical reporting rule:

All policy comparisons should be paired by root snippet, target, candidate seed,
and horizon; report mean, median, bootstrap confidence intervals, and per-scene
win rates for \(J_e^{(H)}\), \(G_t^{(H)}\), and invalidity.

This is especially important because the thesis may operate on a subset if full 100-scene scale is blocked.

⸻

12. Roadmap and risks: strong; add an advisor decision box near the front

The risk section is well written: if M1 geometry/oracle labels fail, the thesis becomes validation + one-step scoring; if target matching is sparse/ambiguous, report target RRI only on validated subsets; if \Delta_{\text{look}} is near zero, report no measurable non-myopic headroom for the evaluated setup. The open advisor decisions are also narrow and appropriate.  ￼

Move the “open advisor decisions” near the front, ideally as a boxed list after the thesis claim:

Advisor decisions requested:
1. target-match acceptance protocol,
2. final scene-level split,
3. first actor-visible crop descriptor,
4. CORAL-to-\(Q_H\) interface,
5. final evidence scale / subset rule,
6. escalation rule for online-discrete or continuous control.

This will make the handout more useful in the actual meeting.

⸻

Research sources to add or reposition

A. Add SCONE for surface-coverage lookahead, but keep it as contrast

SCONE is a useful source to add because it tries to maximize surface metrics by Monte Carlo integration over a volumetric representation and uses attention to predict visibility/gain for candidate poses in large scenes. It supports your argument that candidate utility can be learned over volumetric/point evidence, but it is coverage/surface-gain oriented, not target point-mesh RRI.  ￼

Use it for:

SCONE motivates candidate visibility/gain prediction over volumetric evidence,
but ARIA-NBV keeps point-mesh target-RRI as the supervised utility.

Suggested BibTeX key: SCONE-guedon2022.

B. Add MACARONS for online RGB-only mapping as boundary, not core

MACARONS learns mapping and coverage anticipation from RGB online self-supervision and is relevant to “what if we want online/RGB-only exploration later.” It is useful as a bridge source, not as thesis-core evidence, because your thesis relies on ASE mesh-supervised oracle target-RRI.  ￼

Use it for:

MACARONS is a bridge reference for online/RGB-only coverage anticipation; it
does not replace mesh-supervised target-RRI labels.

Suggested BibTeX key: MACARONS-guedon2023.

C. Update Hestia citation to WACV 2026 accepted paper

Your handout already cites Hestia, but the accepted WACV 2026 open-access entry is stronger than just a project page. The WACV page says Hestia improves RL-based five-degree-of-freedom viewpoint prediction using a hierarchical structure, close-greedy strategy, face-aware design, and reports real-time inference plus robustness to object placement.  ￼

Use it to justify only the post-Q_H bridge:

Hestia motivates target/look-at then feasible-pose factorization and directional
face/visibility memory, but ARIA-NBV does not adopt its coverage reward as the
thesis objective.

D. Keep Set Transformer, but add a simpler baseline

Set Transformer is appropriate because candidate tables are unordered sets and interactions among candidate rows matter. But to avoid overclaiming, add DeepSets or a masked candidate MLP baseline. Your references.bib already appears to include DeepSets and Set Transformer, so this is mostly a writing change. Set Transformer’s own motivation is permutation-invariant set processing with attention-based interactions.  ￼

Use it for:

Permutation-equivariant candidate reasoning is justified, but the required
ablation is no-interaction candidate scoring vs pooled-set interaction.

E. Keep Dueling DQN, but say why it fits finite candidates

Dueling DQN is well aligned because it decomposes value and advantage and is especially useful when many actions have similar values. Your proposal’s finite candidate table will often contain many plausible near-duplicates, so this is a very good source.  ￼

Suggested proposal sentence:

The dueling head is justified because finite candidate tables often contain
many similar-valued actions; the value stream captures scene-target-history
context while the advantage stream captures candidate-specific corrections.

F. Add prioritized replay only if rare high-RRI transitions are a real issue

I would not add prioritized replay as core. But if rollout traces are extremely imbalanced, you can cite it as an ablation for rare high-return transitions. Keep it optional.

Suggested language:

If high-RRI or high-headroom transitions are rare, prioritized sampling of replay
rows is an ablation, not a default training assumption.

G. Use object-centric 3DGS NBV as motivation, not methodology

The object-centric 3DGS NBV preprint is useful because it independently supports target/object-specific view selection in cluttered scenes, but it should not reshape the thesis toward 3DGS. The paper is recent and target-relevant, but its representation and task setup differ from your ASE/EVL point-mesh RRI setting. The search result describes object-centric NBV for object-aware 3DGS in cluttered scenes, focusing views on target objects and reporting depth-error reductions.  ￼

Use it for:

Recent object-centric 3DGS NBV supports the importance of target-conditioned
view utility, but ARIA-NBV uses EVL/ASE point-mesh target-RRI rather than 3DGS
uncertainty as supervision.

⸻

Proposed RQ sharpening

I would keep six RQs, but make them maximally crisp:

RQ1 Objective and metrics:
Can target-conditioned finite-candidate NBV improve endpoint target quality
under equal budget while training on additive target-RRI returns?
RQ2 Target and matching:
Can actor-visible target descriptors and deterministic GT matching produce
leakage-safe target-RRI labels at sufficient coverage?
RQ3 Candidate and rollout support:
Do mixed target-centric/exploration candidates and stochastic rollout support
produce enough valid, diverse, non-myopic training data?
RQ4 Oracle headroom and \(Q_H\):
Does bounded oracle lookahead expose non-myopic headroom, and can masked
residual dueling \(Q_H\) recover it over the learned myopic scorer?
RQ5 Scaling:
Which scale path preserves the same mesh/oracle target-RRI contract beyond
small trusted subsets?
RQ6 Escalation:
Only after RQ1-RQ5 pass, is online discrete interaction or continuous
target-then-pose control scientifically justified?

This is very close to what you have, but it emphasizes “sufficient coverage” and “non-myopic training data” in RQ2/RQ3, which are likely the real thesis risks.

⸻

Suggested objective rewrite

Current objective is implied across the handout. I would make it explicit as:

The objective is not to build a general continuous-control NBV agent. The
objective is to test whether the existing ASE/EVL/VIN substrate can support a
leakage-safe target-conditioned finite-candidate planning result. The required
evidence is: validated target-RRI labels, actor-visible target matching,
a calibrated myopic target scorer, measured oracle-lookahead headroom, and an
oracle-evaluated actor-visible \(Q_{H,\theta}\) policy that recovers measurable
headroom when such headroom exists.

This removes ambiguity and makes your advisor-facing claim very hard to misread.

⸻

Concrete edits I would make now

1. Fix CORAL Eq. 20: replace softmax with sigmoid threshold probabilities and cumulative-to-marginal conversion. This is the only clear mathematical bug I see.  ￼
2. Move advisor decisions to page 1: final split, target-match thresholds, CORAL-to-Q_H, crop descriptor, evidence scale, escalation substrate.  ￼
3. Rename “MDP” to “masked finite-horizon candidate-decision process,” then say it becomes an MDP under fixed generator/RNG/root assumptions.
4. Collapse the value-model section into Core / Ablations / Bridges:
    * Core: target scorer, residual dueling Q_H, masked Double-Q, Set Transformer or candidate-set attention.
    * Ablations: QCNet RPE, S^2 memory, spherical harmonics, distributional heads, GNNs.
    * Bridges: online discrete, continuous target-then-pose, simulator-backed actor-critic.
5. Add SCONE and MACARONS as “coverage/online contrast” sources, not thesis-core methods.  ￼
6. Update Hestia citation to the WACV 2026 open-access paper.  ￼
7. Add area-weighting / surface-sampling caveat for target-mesh completeness.
8. Define all target-match thresholds as advisor decisions rather than leaving matching purely descriptive.
9. Add paired statistical reporting: paired by root snippet, target, seed, candidate budget, horizon; report confidence intervals and scene-level win rates.
10. Clarify training data for Q_H: all valid candidates for one-step labels; only expanded/materialized successor rows for bootstrapped finite-horizon targets.

⸻

Bottom line

The proposal is scientifically coherent and much more mature than the earlier question drafts. The thesis spine is now defensible: quality-driven, target-conditioned, finite-candidate planning under strict leakage controls. The main next step is not to add more architecture. It is to make the proposal sharper by marking the minimal success path:

\text{target-RRI} \rightarrow
\text{actor-visible target descriptor} \rightarrow
\text{myopic scorer} \rightarrow
\Delta_{\text{look}} \rightarrow
Q_{H,\theta}\text{ recovery}

Everything else—QCNet-style RPE, S^2 memory, spherical harmonics, GNNs, distributional heads, IQL, continuous target-then-pose, 3DGS, SceneScript—should be clearly labeled as ablation or bridge, not the thesis success criterion.

# Restore Correct Rerun `Mesh3D` Logging

## Summary
Use Rerun `Mesh3D` again for `/world/gt/mesh`. The correct transparency mechanism is `albedo_factor=[r, g, b, a]`; sampled surface points and wireframe helpers should be removed. The repo currently pins `rerun-sdk==0.22.1`, whose Python `Mesh3D` does **not** support the newer `face_rendering` argument shown in current docs, so this pass should stay compatible with the pinned SDK and not invent unsupported kwargs.

Research basis:
- Rerun `Mesh3D` is the intended archetype for triangle meshes and supports `albedo_factor`; current docs also state transparency ordering assumes counter-clockwise front faces: [Mesh3D docs](https://rerun.io/docs/reference/types/archetypes/mesh3d).
- Installed SDK `0.22.1` supports `albedo_factor` but not `face_rendering`.
- Rerun `Opacity` is a generic component and current docs do not list it as used by `Mesh3D`; do not rely on it for mesh transparency: [Opacity docs](https://rerun.io/docs/reference/types/components/opacity).

## Key Changes
- Revert `/world/gt/mesh` logging to:
  ```python
  rr.Mesh3D(
      vertex_positions=verts.astype(np.float32),
      triangle_indices=faces.astype(np.uint32),
      albedo_factor=[130, 138, 150, mesh_alpha],
  )
  ```
  with `static=True`.
- Remove the sampled-surface-point and wireframe fallback code:
  - delete `_mesh_surface_points`;
  - remove `mesh_surface_point_radius`;
  - remove `max_mesh_surface_points`;
  - remove any tests expecting `Points3D` or `LineStrips3D` for `ENTITY_MESH`.
- Keep `mesh_alpha` as the sole mesh visibility knob. Use `mesh_alpha = 18` as the default/configured value for now, because `51` was too visually dominant.
- Do not log `OpacityBatch` for the mesh. It is not the documented `Mesh3D` transparency path.
- Do not pass `face_rendering` in this pass, because the pinned SDK rejects it. If we later upgrade Rerun, add a separate compatibility pass for `MeshFaceRendering.Front` or current `TransparentFillMajorWireframe` viewer behavior.

## Tests And Verification
- Update `tests/rerun_inspector/test_loggers.py` so `ENTITY_MESH` is logged through `Mesh3D` and preserves the configured alpha in `albedo_factor`.
- Run:
  ```bash
  cd /home/jd/repos/ARIA-NBV/aria_nbv
  uv run ruff format aria_nbv/rerun_inspector/_config.py aria_nbv/rerun_inspector/_loggers.py tests/rerun_inspector/test_loggers.py
  uv run ruff check aria_nbv/rerun_inspector/_config.py aria_nbv/rerun_inspector/_loggers.py tests/rerun_inspector/test_loggers.py
  uv run pytest tests/rerun_inspector/test_loggers.py -q
  ```
- Regenerate the smoke recording:
  ```bash
  uv run nbv-rerun-inspect \
    --config-path ../.configs/rerun_offline.toml \
    --rollout-store ../.data/offline_cache/rollouts_v1_smoke.zarr \
    --rollout-index 0 \
    --rollout-context required \
    --save ../.artifacts/rerun/rollout_v1_smoke.rrd
  ```

- **Known issue:** existing `.rrd` is stale for the installed Rerun reader and must be regenerated.
- **Hypothesis:** 32 candidates over 5 source rows is enough for a first evidence microset, but not a training-scale claim.

## Key Changes
- Add a new microset config, leaving the existing fast smoke config intact:
  - `.configs/build_rollouts_v1_microset.toml`
  - scan `5` VIN offline source rows;
  - `target_selector.k = 3`;
  - fixed candidate budget `32`;
  - mixture counts: `12 TARGET_POINT`, `8 RADIAL_TOWARDS`, `8 RADIAL_AWAY`, `4 FORWARD_RIG`;
  - enable `include_scene_rri = true`;
  - write to `.data/offline_cache/rollouts_v1_microset.zarr`.

- Acceptance bar:
  - at least `1` label-valid V1 target is enough for this debug/evidence tracer;
  - every skipped source/target must have explicit reason accounting;
  - target RRI must be finite and mask-consistent;
  - scene RRI must be finite where audit scoring is enabled;
  - selected candidates must satisfy actor masks;
  - reward dynamic range is reported, but tiny RRI is diagnostic, not failure.

- Visual QA:
  - regenerate fresh `.rrd` artifacts from the new store;
  - produce screenshots with current Rerun CLI, not stale recordings;
  - inspect at least one normal selected rollout and, if present, one boundary case with many invalid candidates or weak target support.

- Cleanup scope:
  - fix only evidence-blocking slop: crashes, stale fallbacks, hidden invalidity, broken metadata, unreadable Rerun output, or unclear skip accounting;
  - do not continue broad rollout/data-handling simplification in this pass unless directly required for evidence validity.

## Theory Contract
The pass validates the data needed for the finite-candidate NBV surrogate:

$$
s_t \rightarrow \mathcal{Q}_t,\quad
a_t \in \{i : m_{t,i}=1\},\quad
r_t^e = \mathrm{RRI}_e(q_{t,a_t})
$$

The evidence store is acceptable only if:
- actor-visible target fields define the target input;
- GT target crop is label/evaluation only;
- invalidity is encoded by masks/reasons, not low RRI;
- target RRI and scene RRI are separate audit signals;
- stored selected transitions can later derive `Q_H` training views.

## Test Plan
Run before and after any code/config changes:

```bash
cd aria_nbv
uv run nbv-build-rollouts --config-path ../.configs/build_rollouts_v1_smoke.toml --dry-run
uv run pytest tests/rollouts tests/data_handling/test_target_selection.py tests/rerun_inspector/test_rollout_zarr_logger.py -q
```

Generate and validate the microset:

```bash

uv run nbv-build-rollouts --config-path ../.configs/build_rollouts_v1_microset.toml
```

Inspect store facts with `RolloutZarrStoreReader.validate()` and a compact table summary:
- counts for sources, targets, rollouts, steps, candidates;
- valid/invalid target counts;
- selected-invalid count must be `0`;
- `q_train_mask` rows must have finite `target_rri`;
- scene-RRI finite count must be reported.

Generate fresh Rerun evidence:

```bash

uv run nbv-rerun-inspect --config-path ../.configs/rerun_offline.toml \
  --rollout-store ../.data/offline_cache/rollouts_v1_microset.zarr \
  --rollout-index 0 \
  --rollout-context required \
  --save ../.artifacts/rerun/rollout_v1_microset_000.rrd

uv run rerun rrd print ../.artifacts/rerun/rollout_v1_microset_000.rrd

uv run rerun ../.artifacts/rerun/rollout_v1_microset_000.rrd \
  --hide-welcome-screen \
  --window-size 1920x1080 \
  --screenshot-to ../.artifacts/rerun/screens/rollout_v1_microset_000.png
```

Finish with:

```bash
cd aria_nbv
uv run ruff check <touched files>
uv run pytest tests/rollouts tests/data_handling/test_target_selection.py tests/rerun_inspector tests/app/panels -q
cd ..
make check-agent-memory
git diff --check
```

## Scenarios
- Normal: one source row yields a matched actor-visible target, finite target/scene RRI, valid selected transitions, and a readable Rerun screenshot with target OBB highlighted.
- Boundary: a source row yields weak support, many invalid candidates, or tiny target-RRI spread; it remains valid if masks, reasons, and geometry are coherent.
- Failure: no label-valid target or unreadable Rerun output; record skip/failure reason and fix the generator/inspector before producing more data.

## Assumptions
- This microset is smoke/evidence, not training-scale data.
- Existing `rollouts.zarr` schema stays unless validation exposes an evidence-blocking flaw.
- Generated `.zarr`, `.rrd`, and screenshots remain local artifacts unless explicitly requested for tracking.
- Full-scale sharding, LRZ/DSS, Gumbel branches, and `Q_H` training are follow-up work after this microset is trusted.

(^1) According to a document from 2026-05-13, the updated proposal is now much stronger: it has a defensible thesis spine, a conditional success rule, a leakage-aware comparison table, and a clear separation between thesis-core finite-candidate $Q_H$ and later continuous/simulator work. The main remaining opportunity is **not** to add more architectural components; it is to make the architecture read like a principled geometric-ML design derived from the symmetries of the task. ## High-level review The updated proposal’s best move is the conditional framing: ARIA-NBV first tests whether oracle lookahead actually creates measurable non-myopic headroom. If $\Delta_{\text{look}} > 0$, $Q_H$ must recover some of that headroom over the learned myopic target scorer; if $\Delta_{\text{look}} \approx 0$, the thesis reports a negative planning result for the evaluated candidate distribution, horizon, branch factor, target set, and split instead of “rescuing” the story with architecture changes. That is scientifically mature and should stay central. The research-question chain is also good: objective and metrics $\rightarrow$ target matching $\rightarrow$ candidate support $\rightarrow$ lookahead/$Q_H$ $\rightarrow$ scaling $\rightarrow$ online/continuous escalation. That dependency structure protects the thesis from becoming a bag of ideas. The evidence contract is similarly strong: it requires rank correlation, top-$k$ oracle hit, calibration, stage-shift diagnostics, validity masks, reason codes, shuffled-candidate evaluation, paired policy comparisons, bootstrap confidence intervals, and per-scene win rates. The part I would sharpen is the **architectural rationale**. Right now, the proposal lists many reasonable modules: R6D+LFF pose features, $\mathbb{S}^2$ directional memory, MLP/DeepSets/Set Transformer comparisons, QCNet-style relative positional encoding, spherical-harmonic memory, edge-conditioned spatial GNNs, distributional heads, and privileged-teacher distillation. This is technically rich, but it risks reading like “architecture soup” unless you explicitly derive each module from an invariance, equivariance, or data-generation bottleneck. ## The geometric-deep-learning sharpened thesis aim I would rephrase the thesis aim as: > ARIA-NBV tests whether target-conditioned, quality-driven egocentric NBV can be reduced to a leakage-safe finite-candidate decision problem whose value model respects the permutation symmetry of candidate sets, the Euclidean structure of camera/target geometry, the spherical nature of directional observability, and the oracle/actor split between privileged supervision and deployable inputs. That sentence does three things. It keeps the existing $Q_H$ spine; it invokes geometric deep learning without overclaiming; and it turns “architecture choices” into testable inductive biases. This aligns well with Bronstein et al.’s geometric deep learning blueprint, which argues that architectures should exploit task regularities from the low-dimensional and structured physical world, and that geometric principles give a constructive way to encode prior physical knowledge. ([arXiv][1]) ## Symmetry and inductive-bias contract Your model has four different geometric objects, and each needs a different bias. | Object | Mathematical structure | Desired property | Thesis-safe implementation | | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------: | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Candidate table $\mathcal Q_t={q_{t,i}}$ | finite set | permutation equivariance: permuting rows permutes $Q_i$ outputs | MLP baseline, DeepSets, Set Transformer / masked self-attention | | Camera/target/history poses | $SE(3)$ / gravity-aligned $SE(2.5)$ | invariance to global coordinate choice; equivariance of relative vectors | rig- or candidate-local frames, R6D rotations, relative pose features, optional EGNN | | Directional visibility | $\mathbb S^2$ | remember *which directions* have already observed target-local cells | second-moment matrix, spherical histogram, low-order spherical harmonics | | Target identity | selected entity / OBB crop | target is a query/gauge, not just metadata | target-local ROI read from actor-visible scene memory | This is the architecture story I recommend adding. It is cleaner than saying “we use a Transformer because it is powerful.” Deep Sets is the canonical baseline for permutation-invariant/equivariant set functions, while Set Transformer adds attention-based interactions among set elements and an inducing-point scheme to reduce self-attention cost. ([NeurIPS Papers][2]) Your proposal already requires MLP/DeepSets/Set Transformer controls before attributing gains to Set Transformer or QCNet-style RPE; keep that as a hard experimental rule. ## A more elegant architecture I would **not** make the first $Q_H$ a large 3D backbone. The elegant version is a small relational decision model on top of the expensive EVL/oracle substrate: ```text actor-visible state: frozen EVL root field F_0^EVL accumulated point proxy P_t actor-visible target record z_e selected-view history h_t candidate table Q_t, mask m_t, reason rho_t stage A: calibrated myopic scorer r_hat_e(s_t, z_e, q_i) stage B: candidate token x_i = pose/target features frustum/belief features directional novelty validity/reason embedding history summary strategy provenance stage C: permutation-equivariant candidate interaction E_set({x_i}, m_t) stage D: residual dueling value head: Q_H(s_t,z_e,q_i) = r_hat_e(s_t,z_e,q_i) + V_theta(s_t,z_e,h_t) + A_theta,i^H - mean_valid_j A_theta,j^H ``` That is already essentially in the handout, but I would make it the *only* main architecture. The current document says $Q_H$ is residual around the calibrated myopic base, uses CORAL-to-expected-RRI decoding, and trains the myopic base before freezing or slow-finetuning it for residual $Q_H$. This is good because it gives a clear ablation: “Does finite-horizon residual value learning add anything beyond calibrated one-step target RRI?” ### Where to use equivariance Use equivariance **surgically**, not everywhere. A lightweight EGNN-style candidate graph is attractive for an ablation because EGNNs are designed to be equivariant to rotations, translations, reflections, and permutations without requiring expensive higher-order tensor representations. ([Proceedings of Machine Learning Research][3]) For ARIA-NBV, that suggests an ablation where candidate centers, target centers, and history centers are graph nodes with scalar node features and relative displacement messages. But this should be a post-MLP/DeepSets/Set-Transformer ablation, not the default first implementation. SE(3)-Transformer/e3nn-style tensor features are conceptually beautiful but probably too heavy for the thesis core. SE(3)-Transformer gives roto-translation equivariant attention over point clouds/graphs, and e3nn is an official PyTorch library for $O(3)$-equivariant neural networks. ([arXiv][4]) I would reserve them for a small, well-isolated “directional-memory / target-local crop” ablation, not the whole candidate scorer. ### A clean “geometric ML” ablation ladder Run exactly this ladder, with fixed seeds/splits/schedules: 1. **No-interaction candidate MLP**: each candidate scored independently. 2. **DeepSets pooled context**: candidate gets global valid-set summary. 3. **Set Transformer / masked self-attention**: candidate-candidate interactions. 4. **QCNet-style local-frame RPE**: relations expressed in candidate $i$’s frame. 5. **EGNN candidate graph**: equivariant message passing over candidate/target/history points. 6. **$\mathbb S^2$ memory ablations**: none vs second moment vs histogram vs low-order spherical harmonics. QCNet is relevant only for its query-centric design ethos and local-frame relative encoding. The CVPR paper’s core idea is to learn representations independent of the global spacetime coordinate system and reuse invariant scene features; do not import its trajectory-decoding losses or autonomous-driving claims. ([CVF Open Access][5]) This boundary already matches your literature ledger. ## Directional memory: make it a thesis contribution, not just a feature The proposal’s $\mathbb S^2$ directional memory is one of the best ideas. It separates candidate orientation from accumulated observation history, which is exactly the kind of inductive bias this problem needs. Your handout already distinguishes query-centric RPE as a pose-relation signal from $\mathbb S^2$ memory as an accumulated visibility signal. I would make the directional-memory question sharper: > Does target-local directional observability improve non-myopic target-RRI recovery beyond target-relative pose and current frustum evidence? Then test: [ M_{\mathrm{dir}}(v)= \sum_{k<t} w_k(v)d_k(v)d_k(v)^\top ] against: [ h_{\mathrm{dir}}(v)=\sum_{k<t} w_k(v)Y_L(d_k(v)). ] The second-moment memory is elegant because it is cheap, symmetric positive semidefinite, interpretable, and does not require committing to e3nn. The spherical-harmonic version is the principled ablation. e3nn is a credible implementation reference for spherical harmonics and equivariant components. ([docs.e3nn.org][6]) ## Better data generation: move from “more labels” to “support coverage” The biggest empirical risk is not architecture. It is whether the rollout dataset covers enough target/candidate/history configurations to make $Q_H$ meaningful. The handout already says the bootstrapped $Q_H$ backup should only train on expanded transition rows where selected action, successor state, successor candidate table, successor mask, and terminal flag are materialized. Make this a named data-generation aim: > Generate transition support, not just more one-step labels. Recommended data products: | Data product | Purpose | Minimum evidence | | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | one-step all-candidate labels | train/calibrate $\hat r^e_\psi$ | rank correlation, top-$k$, calibration | | paired greedy/lookahead roots | measure $\Delta_{\text{look}}$ | same root, target, seed, $N_q$, $H$ | | stochastic support traces | avoid Q-learning over only greedy states | entropy, unique selected chains, target visibility | | hard negatives / invalid near-misses | teach masks and failure modes | invalid reason distribution | | multi-anchor snippets | reduce overfitting to “last-frame only” | anchor-time stratification | | multi-candidate-set augmentation | test candidate-distribution dependence | per-strategy RRI histograms | | target strata | avoid only easy/large targets | class, support, projected area, occlusion bins | The current proposal already uses temperature-softmax for support widening and keeps Gumbel-Top-$K$ as a later diversity method if temperature-softmax is insufficient. I would make the trigger explicit: adopt Gumbel-Top-$K$ only when effective sample size or unique-chain diversity stays low. ### Candidate generation should be experimental, not incidental Right now the first candidate mixture is target/look-at, radial-towards/radial-away, forward-rig, and bounded jitter. That is a good starting point, but the thesis should report candidate-generator sensitivity because a “no non-myopic headroom” result may simply mean the candidate distribution is too myopic. Add these candidate families as controlled strata: 1. **Target look-at shells** around predicted OBB center / support centroid. 2. **Occlusion-bypass candidates**: lateral offsets around target-bearing ray. 3. **Doorway/frontier candidates**: only as a bridge if target is not visible. 4. **Revisit/refinement candidates**: high expected target detail, small movement. 5. **Exploration candidates**: radial/forward-rig mix. 6. **Hard invalid/near-invalid candidates**: for validity robustness, not for reward learning. Do not mix them silently. Store `strategy_id`, target-bearing angle, path increment, predicted visibility, invalid reason, and current target support. ## Data generation inspiration from other systems GenNBV is useful mainly as a data-diversity lesson. It uses continuous 5-DoF actions, multi-source state embeddings, a probabilistic 3D grid, semantic representation, action history, and large simulator training; but its reward is coverage gain, not target RRI. The transferable idea is not PPO—it is **diverse training environments and state embeddings that distinguish occupied/free/unknown**, plus action-history conditioning. GenNBV’s own experiments emphasize cross-dataset generalization and ablate multi-source state embeddings and depth-based 3D representations. VIN-NBV remains the core objective precedent because it predicts RRI directly, uses 3D-aware featurization, visibility count, normals, depth, and an empty-pixel/coverage feature, and trains via ordinal RRI labels. Your current proposal correctly treats VIN-NBV as the one-step/myopic control, not as proof of multi-step planning. SCONE and MACARONS should be written as contrastive data-generation references: SCONE combines volumetric occupancy prediction with surface-coverage integration to scale to large scenes and free camera motion, while MACARONS learns RGB-only occupancy and NBV prediction with online self-supervision. ([NeurIPS Proceedings][7]) ARIA-NBV should borrow their “predict support/visibility cheaply before expensive scoring” pattern, but not replace mesh-supervised target-RRI with coverage. For external generation, ProcTHOR is useful as evidence that procedural diversity can scale embodied-agent training: it procedurally samples diverse, interactive, customizable, performant 3D environments and reports a 10,000-house sample. ([arXiv][8]) But ProcTHOR/AI2-THOR should be a semantic/global-planning sidecar, not the main ARIA/RRI renderer, because your core depends on Aria-like cameras, MPS-style semidense products, EVL compatibility, and GT mesh/OBB supervision. Isaac Sim is the more plausible public sensor-fidelity route because current docs include camera, depth, lidar/radar, IMU, contact, and other sensor simulation extensions. ([Isaac Sim Documentation][9]) Habitat is the better fast sidecar for geometry/navigation rollouts because Habitat-Sim is designed as a high-performance configurable-agent/sensor simulator and reports very high rendering throughput. ([AI Meta][10]) ## Better architecture ideas from spatial ML ### 1. Candidate graph instead of monolithic Transformer Represent one decision step as a heterogeneous graph: [ \mathcal G_t=(V_{\text{cand}}\cup V_{\text{target}}\cup V_{\text{hist}}\cup V_{\text{cell}},E). ] Edges carry relative geometry: [ e_{j\to i}= \left[ R_i^\top(p_j-c_i), |p_j-c_i|, \operatorname{enc}(R_i^\top R_j), \Delta t, \mathrm{strategy}_j \right]. ] Then use: * MLP edges + attention as default, * EGNN as an equivariant ablation, * Set Transformer as the strong non-equivariant candidate-set baseline. This gives you a clean answer to “why this architecture?” The candidate is the query; target/history/cells are relational context; output is one value per valid candidate. ### 2. Target-local ROI token is mandatory Your proposal already says the target token should not be just a descriptor; it should read actor-visible target-local scene memory via ROIAlign3D over the observed/predicted OBB, not a GT crop. I would elevate this from “implementation detail” to “leakage-safe target grounding.” The target descriptor alone can encode object identity and geometry, but the ROI feature tells the model what is currently known, unknown, and directionally observed around that target. ### 3. Sparse scene updates are a scaling ablation, not core Sparse convolution backbones are credible if dense EVL/voxel updates become memory-bound. MinkowskiEngine is an official sparse-tensor autodiff library that supports standard sparse layers such as convolution, pooling, unpooling, and broadcasting. ([GitHub][11]) Point Transformer V3 is also a good implementation reference if you later need a scalable point backbone: its paper explicitly prioritizes simplicity/efficiency and reports large receptive-field scaling and multi-dataset training benefits. ([arXiv][12]) KPConv is a trustworthy older point-cloud reference because it operates directly on point clouds using kernel points in Euclidean space and has deformable variants that adapt to local geometry. ([CVF Open Access][13]) But for the thesis core, I would **not** replace the current EVL + compact candidate-token pipeline with a full point backbone. Use PTv3/KPConv/Minkowski only if the experiment asks: “Does a stronger accumulated-geometry encoder improve target-RRI ranking after all simpler relational/candidate-set baselines are controlled?” ### 4. Privileged teacher distillation is promising You have a strict actor/oracle split, which is good. But privileged oracle fields can still supervise an actor-visible student. A clean formulation: [ Q^{\text{teacher}}_H(s^{\text{oracle}}_t,z_e,q_i) \rightarrow Q^{\text{student}}_H(s^{\text{cf0}}_t,z_e,q_i). ] Allowed teacher inputs: all-candidate renders, GT target mesh crop, GT visibility, true candidate target support. Allowed student inputs: EVL root, accumulated actor-visible geometry, observed/predicted target record, selected history, candidate table, masks/reasons. Loss: [ \mathcal L = \mathcal L_{\text{DoubleQ}} + \lambda_{\text{distill}} \sum_{i:m_i=1} \left( \tilde Q^{\text{student}}_i-\tilde Q^{\text{teacher}}_i \right)^2. ] This is scientifically elegant because it acknowledges that the oracle knows more, without leaking privileged state into the final policy. ## Sharpened thesis contributions I would reduce the proposal’s contributions to four: 1. **Leakage-safe target-RRI protocol.** Actor-visible target selection and predicted-target $Q$ inputs; GT crops only for matching, labels, and evaluation. 2. **Headroom-measured finite-candidate planning.** Paired oracle-1 vs oracle-lookahead defines whether non-myopic planning is useful for the chosen candidate distribution. 3. **Geometry-aware residual $Q_H$.** A candidate-set-equivariant residual dueling value model built around calibrated myopic target-RRI, with explicit directional memory and local-frame relation ablations. 4. **Support-aware data generation.** Stochastic, replayable, target-stratified, candidate-stratified rollout traces with validity masks and successor candidate tables, not just more one-step labels. Everything else—continuous target-then-pose, Habitat/Isaac, 3DGS/Fisher, SceneScript/VLM—is a bridge or discussion section unless it directly improves one of those four contributions. ## Specific things to add to the proposal Add a short subsection titled **“Geometric inductive-bias contract.”** Suggested text: ```text The value model is not a generic Transformer over arbitrary features. It is designed around four task symmetries: candidate-row permutation equivariance, Euclidean relative geometry, target-local gauge conditioning, and spherical directional observability. The ablation ladder tests these biases in increasing order of complexity: independent candidate MLP, DeepSets pooled context, masked Set Transformer, candidate-local relative positional encoding, and optional equivariant candidate graph. A module is thesis-core only if it improves oracle-evaluated endpoint target quality under the paired headroom protocol. ``` Add a short subsection titled **“Support coverage in rollout generation.”** Suggested text: ```text The rollout store is evaluated not only by sample count but by support coverage: target classes/support bins, candidate strategy provenance, valid/invalid reason histograms, unique selected chains, successor candidate-table availability, and per-scene coverage. Bootstrapped Q_H targets are trained only where successor counterfactual states and masks are materialized; non-expanded rows remain one-step supervision. ``` Add a sentence to the architecture section: ```text The default model uses scalar invariant and local-frame relative features rather than full SE(3)-equivariant tensor features; equivariant graph or spherical-harmonic modules are controlled ablations motivated by the geometric deep learning blueprint, not prerequisites for thesis success. ``` ## Things to cut or demote Demote **distributional $Q_H$**, **CQL/IQL/BCQ**, **full sparse/point backbone swaps**, and **continuous actor-critic** to “M6/M7 only if M5 succeeds.” The current literature ledger already says IQL/CQL/BCQ and distributional heads are later ablations, and that GenNBV/Hestia/3DGS/SceneScript should not replace target point-mesh RRI. Do not make the thesis depend on a simulator. Your current handout is right: online discrete interaction and continuous target-then-pose control are scaling/escalation questions after the finite-candidate result. The external simulator question should be framed as: “Which substrate preserves comparable target-RRI supervision?” not “Which simulator is coolest?” ## Strong final positioning The thesis will be sharper if it says: > We do not claim that bigger neural architectures solve NBV. We first ask whether the finite candidate distribution contains non-myopic target-RRI headroom. If it does, we test whether a small geometry-aware, permutation-equivariant residual value model can recover that headroom under oracle re-evaluation. If it does not, we report a negative planning result and identify whether the bottleneck is target matching, candidate support, or supervision scale. That is a strong scientific claim because it can succeed, fail, or produce a useful negative result without changing the rules midstream.
